turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through and grab a seat. What's brought you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, it's this ringing in the right ear, doctor. Been at me for a month or so. I don't know, I can't put a date on when it actually started.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Is the ringing there all the time?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, all the time. Worse when it's dead quiet, like once the telly's off at night.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the hearing on that side, does it feel dull or muffled?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the right one. Feels like I've got cotton wool stuffed in there. I don't know, doctor, it's hard to put into words.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the ear?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fluid or discharge coming out of it?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Down at the shop the machines are so loud I can't hear myself think. I've overdone it with the overtime, that's the truth of it.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll get to the shop. Any gunk or fluid from the ear itself?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. No, nothing coming out.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any dizziness, or the room spinning?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah. I'm steady on my feet.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about your breathing or your chest, any trouble there?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Chest is fine, breathing's normal.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): What sort of work are you doing?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Metal fabrication. Presses and grinders going all day, loud as anything.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ear muffs or plugs at all?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor, I pretty much never wear them. They get sweaty, so they live in the locker.

[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ok, so I'm turning this over. Loud noise can rattle the tiny hearing cells, and they keep firing after the noise stops, which is why a ring often feels louder once the room goes quiet.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): So I've wrecked the ear, have I?

[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not wrecked, I don't think. My working impression is noise-related tinnitus. Whether there's actual hearing loss as well, from the noise or from wax, I can't separate those yet.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm. There is a bit of wax, I reckon.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me have a look. Right canal's got a moderate plug of wax. The drum behind it isn't red, and it isn't bulging.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Right.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Left ear is clear, and that drum looks normal.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure today is one thirty two over eighty four, pulse is seventy six. Both sitting fine.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): That's alright then.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any regular medicines?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the cholesterol tablet. Atorvastin, err, twenty milligrams at night.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the high cholesterol is still an ongoing thing?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Been on it five-ish years. I don't know, doctor, I lose track.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. I'm going to refer you for an audiogram, a proper hearing test with audiology.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to go? I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. Err, it'll tell us if the muffling is the wax, the noise, or a bit of both. I'll send the request through today.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): From now on, muffs on every time those presses or grinders are running. Even the short jobs add up.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, I'll pull them out of the locker. Should've done it ages ago.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back and see me in about six weeks, once that hearing test result is in front of us.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Yep, I can do that.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the ringing suddenly roars up, or you get spinning, or a weak face, don't wait it out. Emergency, or straight back here.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I hear you. Thanks, doctor.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): No worries. We'll know more once the test is back.

spec.situation: Ringing in the right ear for a month, worse in quiet; works with loud machinery without ear protection; some muffled hearing; hearing test referral.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.

omissions.text: Patient denied vertigo/room spinning, stating he was steady on his feet.
Vital signs were taken with the patient sitting ('both sitting fine').
Audiogram referral was to be sent through today.
Follow-up was specified as after the hearing test result is available ('come back in about six weeks, once that hearing test result is in front of us').
Safety-net advice included going to emergency or straight back to the clinic if symptoms occur, not just seeking urgent care generally.
